Front: Who argued the Revolution was the work of irresponsible intellectuals against time-honoured institutions?
Back: Edmund Burke (interpretation 1) ·FR p1

Front: Who argued the Revolution was a popular, spontaneous upheaval of the entire French nation?
Back: Jules Michelet (interpretation 3) ·FR p1

Front: Whose reading makes the Revolution a class struggle between landed nobility and bourgeoisie?
Back: Marxist historians (interpretation 4) ·FR p1

Front: Which interpretation makes the Revolution a revolt of respectable middle-class property owners?
Back: Interpretation 2, unattributed in the handout ·FR p1

Front: Which event is the Revolution said to be comparable to in European life?
Back: The Protestant Reformation of the sixteenth century ·FR p1

Front: Which five ideas does the handout say the Revolution released beyond France?
Back: Liberalism, socialism, democracy, fraternity, nationalism ·FR p1

Front: Name the three philosophes the handout cites.
Back: Voltaire, Montesquieu, Rousseau ·FR p1

Front: Give the three limits on the intellectuals' responsibility.
Back: They wanted reform not revolution; there was no organised movement to turn their ideas into a programme; most participants in 1789 were illiterate and had not heard of them ·FR p1

Front: Reign dates of Louis XV and Louis XVI?
Back: Louis XV 1715-1774; Louis XVI 1774-1793 ·FR p2

Front: What was Louis XV more interested in than governing?
Back: Food and women - he left decisions to courtiers who excelled only in flattery and intrigue ·FR p2

Front: Which two wars drained French finances, and when?
Back: War of the Austrian Succession 1740-48; Seven Years War 1756-63 ·FR p2

Front: By what year had the national debt become an intolerable burden?
Who bore the heaviest tax burden under the old regime?
Back: The peasants and the bourgeoisie - the unprivileged orders ·FR p2 (printed 'persons', C8)

Front: Who was Turgot and what happened to him?
Back: Louis XVI's finance minister; proposed removing aristocratic tax exemptions; the nobility and church opposed and the king dismissed him ·FR p2

Front: What did Necker do instead of reforming?
Back: Resorted to more public borrowing to appease the aristocracy ·FR p2

Front: Which foreign intervention deepened the fiscal crisis, and when?
Back: The American War of Independence, 1776-1783 ·FR p2

Front: What is meant by the aristocratic revolt?
Back: The privileged orders' defeat of royal tax reform - the first body to beat the crown was the nobility, not the Third Estate ·FR p2

Front: When had the Estates-General last met before 1789?
What phrase does the handout use for the decision to convene the Estates-General?
Back: An abdication of royal power and an invitation to revolution ·FR p2

Front: What were the three orders?
Back: Clergy (First Estate), Aristocracy (Second Estate), Third Estate or commoners ·FR p2

Front: How were the seats allocated in 1789?
Back: 600 to the Third Estate, 300 each to clergy and nobility ·FR p3

Front: Why was doubling the Third Estate's seats worthless alone?
Back: Because voting by order would still let the other two outvote it 2-1; the concessions only work together ·FR p3

Front: What happened to the price of bread and to Paris unemployment before 1789?
Back: Bread doubled; Paris unemployment rose by 50% ·FR p4

Front: What, rather than economic crisis, precipitated popular intervention?
Back: Fear of counter-revolution - royal troops around Paris and Versailles, and rumours of foreign intervention ·FR p4

Front: What three things did peasants fear in the Great Fear?
Back: Aristocratic conspiracy, foreign invasion, and the intentions of the bourgeoisie ·FR p5

Front: What does the handout conclude about the peasants' role?
Back: They were both allies and potential enemies of the bourgeois revolution ·FR p5

Front: What happened on 17 June 1789?
Back: The Third Estate constituted itself the National Assembly and invited the other orders to join ·FR p3

Front: When did the majority of the clergy vote to join?
Back: 19 June 1789, two days later (V4) ·FR p3

Front: Date and name of the Tennis Court Oath?
Back: 20 June 1789 - the Serment du Jeu de Paume (V2; the handout calls it a 'resolution' and misplaces it) ·FR p3

Front: What did Louis XVI do on 23 June 1789?
Back: Summoned the Estates-General, promised a constitutional monarchy, ordered the orders to meet separately, and ordered the National Assembly dissolved - and was defied ·FR p3

Front: When was the National Assembly renamed, and to what?
Back: July 1789, to the Constituent Assembly ·FR p3

Front: Date and significance of the storming of the Bastille?
Back: 14 July 1789 - symbolised the fall of royal despotism; followed by civilian militias and municipal governments across France ·FR p4

Front: What shifted after 14 July 1789?
Back: Political initiative passed from the National Assembly to the popular forces of the Revolution ·FR p4

Front: When was the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen issued?
Back: August 1789 ·FR p5

Front: Which two influences shaped the reforms of 1789-91?
Back: The French intellectuals' liberal and democratic ideas, and the American Bill of Rights ·FR p5

Front: Name four rights in the Declaration.
Back: Equality before the law; freedom of speech and the press; freedom of conscience; freedom from arbitrary arrest; equitable taxation; the right of rebellion; office by talent not birth; private property ·FR p5-6

Front: On what four subjects was the Declaration silent?
Back: Economic enterprise and trade; popular democracy; freedom of association; slavery and the slave trade ·FR p6

Front: Where did sovereignty rest under the new constitution?
Back: In the nation - that is, in the National Parliament of elected representatives ·FR p6

Front: What three powers did the king retain?
Back: Appointing ministers, ambassadors and commanders; declaring war or making peace with parliamentary consent; suspending or delaying non-financial legislation for up to four years ·FR p6

Front: Which religious minorities gained freedom of worship?
Back: Protestants and Jews ·FR p6

Front: What was done with Church and noble lands?
Back: Divided and redistributed to the peasants ·FR p6

Front: Describe the economic settlement in one line.
Back: Internal free market - tolls and customs posts removed, feudal restrictions swept away - with external tariffs retained to protect national industry ·FR p6-7

Front: Which two old taxes were abolished?
Back: Church tithes and the salt tax ·FR p7

Front: What happened to the government bonds introduced to raise revenue?
Back: They were soon used as bank notes - these are the assignats, which the handout never names ·FR p7

Front: Name the five reasons for the radicalization of the Revolution.
Back: Counter-revolution; royalist plots; the deepening economic crisis; political divisions in the revolutionary camp; the outbreak of war in April 1792 ·FR p7-9

Front: What phrase describes those the Revolution's supporters wanted repressed?
Back: Its enemies, real or imaginary ·FR p7

Front: Which four powers did Louis XVI covertly solicit, 1789-91?
Back: Austria, Prussia, Sweden, Spain ·FR p7

Front: What happened when Louis XVI tried to flee, and when?
Back: June 1791 - the Flight to Varennes; he was arrested and returned to Paris a prisoner, and became more unpopular than ever ·FR p8

Front: What did the radicals demand that the moderates did not?
Back: Universal manhood suffrage and redistribution of wealth to produce economic equality ·FR p8

Front: What did the anti-war politicians of 1791-92 predict?
Back: That war would destroy the essence of the Revolution and lead to military dictatorship - and they were right ·FR p8

Front: Against whom did France declare war in April 1792?
Back: Austria alone, on 20 April 1792; Prussia entered afterwards as its ally (V1 - the handout says 'Prussia and Austria') ·FR p9

Front: When was the First French Republic proclaimed?
What was the Declaration of Pillnitz?
Back: Austria and Prussia's 1791 call to European rulers to help Louis XVI re-establish himself in power ·RNW ¶4

Front: What years do the Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars span?
Back: 1792-1815 in one source; the Napoleonic Wars alone dated 1799-1815 in the other (D1) ·RNW ¶2, ·NW ¶1

Front: When do the revolutionary wars conveniently end, and what changed?
Back: By 1801; with Napoleon's rise to absolute power, war aims reverted to simple aggrandizement of influence and territory ·RNW ¶2

Front: How many coalitions opposed France?
Back: Seven, over 23 years from 1793 ·RNW ¶4

Front: Compare army sizes before and after 1800.
Back: Mid-eighteenth century 60,000-70,000; Napoleon after 1800 routinely 250,000; Russia 1812 some 600,000 ·RNW ¶4

Front: What was the levée en masse?
Back: The decree placing all Frenchmen at the army's disposal, producing armies of unprecedented size ·RNW ¶4

Front: Who commanded at Valmy, when, and against whom?
Back: Dumouriez and Kellermann, 20 September 1792, against a Prussian-Austrian force ·RNW ¶4

Front: Name the First Coalition's members.
Back: Austria, Prussia, Spain, the United Provinces, Great Britain - early 1793 ·RNW ¶4

Front: What did Prussia do in 1795?
Back: Left the coalition and signed a separate peace that held until 1806 ·RNW ¶6

Front: What became the Batavian Republic, and when?
Back: The United Provinces of the Netherlands, May 1795 ·RNW ¶6

Front: When and why was Napoleon given command in Italy?
Back: March 1796, replacing a commander reluctant to move ·RNW ¶6

Front: What did Austria concede at Campo Formio?
Back: The Austrian Netherlands - the Republic's first territorial additions - and recognition of the Cisalpine and Ligurian republics ·RNW ¶7

Front: What ended the Egyptian campaign?
Back: Nelson's destruction of the French squadron at the Battle of the Nile, 1 August 1798, leaving Napoleon without naval support ·RNW ¶8

Front: Where was the Parthenopean Republic?
Back: Naples - not Piedmont, where the client state was the Subalpine Republic (V6) ·RNW ¶8

Front: Name the Second Coalition.
Back: Britain, Russia, the Ottoman Empire, Naples, Portugal, Austria ·RNW ¶8

Front: Date and name of the coup that made Napoleon First Consul?
Back: 18 Brumaire, year VIII - 9 November 1799 ·RNW ¶8

Front: Name three ways Napoleon consolidated his rule.
Back: Suppressed rebellions; the Concordat of 1801 with the Church; the Napoleonic Code ·NW ¶2

Front: When did Napoleon declare himself Emperor?
Match: Marengo, Ulm, Austerlitz, Jena-Auerstädt, Friedland.
What did Tilsit do?
Back: Halved Prussia at the Elbe and took part of its Poland; forced Alexander I into alliance with Napoleon - 1807 ·RNW ¶8, ·NW ¶3

Front: Which four states stayed outside French control after 1809?
Back: Portugal, Sweden, Sardinia, Sicily ·RNW ¶8

Front: Date and significance of Trafalgar?
Back: 21 October 1805 - ended the French threat to invade England; the other source calls it just about the only blemish on Napoleon's record that decade ·RNW ¶8, ·NW ¶3

Front: What was the Berlin Decree, and when?
Back: 1806 - ships calling at British ports before reaching French-controlled ports became liable to seizure; it created the Continental System ·RNW ¶9

Front: Give four reasons the Continental System failed.
Back: British retaliation froze European trade; licences to French merchants looked like favouritism and cost political support; Britain expanded colonial markets and grew richer; it provoked German nationalism and the Spanish Peninsular War ·RNW ¶9, ·NW ¶4

Front: What did enforcing the System produce in Spain?
Back: The Peninsular War - a protracted guerrilla war that diverted French forces from the rest of Europe ·NW ¶4

Front: What were the Spanish guerrillas fighting for?
Back: To return a Bourbon to the throne - a conservative aim, while German opposition wanted more self-rule ·NW ¶11

Front: Describe Napoleon's military method.
Back: Move armies rapidly, strike quickly and often by surprise, prevent his enemies coordinating, and defeat them piecemeal - requiring terrain knowledge and living off requisition ·RNW ¶11

Front: What was the answer his enemies found?
Back: Maintain a threat while avoiding engagement until coordinated, rely on strong supply lines, and let his own overextend ·RNW ¶11

Front: Who used that strategy first, and supplied from where?
Back: Wellington in the Peninsula, supplied through Portugal ·RNW ¶11

Front: Which Russian generals answered the 1812 invasion, and how?
Back: Barclay de Tolly and Bagration - they simply withdrew along parallel lines ·RNW ¶11

Front: What triggered the invasion of Russia?
Back: Alexander I withdrew Russia from the Continental System at the end of 1810 ·NW ¶5

Front: Borodino - date and result?
Back: 7 September 1812; the only full-scale engagement of the campaign, and indecisive, so Napoleon was eventually forced to retreat ·RNW ¶11

Front: What did Napoleon lose in Russia?
Back: 500,000 men, the faith of his allies, and the awe of his enemies ·RNW ¶11

Front: Leipzig - when and what?
Back: October 1813 - defeat by an international coalition of armies ·NW ¶5

Front: When did Napoleon first abdicate, and where was he exiled?
Back: 6 April 1814; exiled to Elba, which lasted less than a year ·RNW ¶12

Front: What were the Hundred Days?
Back: March to June 1815 - Napoleon's return from Elba, the army he raised, and the brief final campaign ·RNW ¶12, ·NW ¶6

Front: Name the Seventh Coalition.
Back: Great Britain, Russia, Prussia, Austria - 1815 ·RNW ¶12

Front: Date of Waterloo, and what happened two days before?
Back: 18 June 1815; on 16 June, Ligny and Quatre Bras - different battles, different places (V5) ·RNW ¶12

Front: Why did Napoleon lose at Waterloo, in the source's analysis?
Back: The same failure as in Russia - he could not surprise, and could not prevent two armies invading along separate lines from joining ·RNW ¶12

Front: Where did Napoleon die?
Back: Saint Helena, in the South Atlantic ·NW ¶6

Front: Name the five Vienna negotiators and their powers.
Back: Metternich (Austria), Castlereagh (Britain), Alexander I (Russia), Hardenberg (Prussia), Talleyrand (France) ·NW ¶7

Front: What did the Congress achieve, and what did it protect?
Back: A balance in which no one power could dominate and rising powers could be stopped by coalitions - and it protected conservative regimes against liberal change ·NW ¶7, ¶14

Front: What conflict did the Congress set the stage for?
Back: Liberalism versus conservatism, 1815 to the revolutionary year 1848 ·NW ¶14

Front: What survived of Napoleon's rule in law?
Back: The Napoleonic Code, imposed on occupied countries, forming the legal basis for much of Continental European law today ·NW ¶10

Front: Which Prussian reformers rebuilt their state on French lines, and why?
Back: Baron Stein and Hardenberg - because to compete with France they had to resemble it ·NW ¶10

Front: Which intellectual movement did Germany champion against French rationalism?
Back: Romanticism ·NW ¶4, ¶11

Front: Why, according to the source, did Britain win the wars?
Back: It emerged in 1815 with a commercial powerhouse economy, the pre-eminent navy and a large colonial network - and national unity against Napoleon carried it through a dangerous phase of its Industrial Revolution ·NW ¶13

Front: Which two New World events echoed the wars?
Back: The War of 1812 and Toussaint l'Ouverture's regime in Haiti ·NW ¶9

Front: What is the source's moral verdict on the period?
Back: That right and wrong are hard to distinguish - Napoleon a dictator but not a particularly evil one, and all sides driven by greed in a period typified by Realism. Treat as interpretation, not fact ·NW ¶12

Front: TRAP: against whom did France declare war in April 1792?
Back: Austria alone, 20 April 1792. The handout says 'Prussia and Austria'. Prussia joined afterwards. (V1)

Front: TRAP: when was the Tennis Court Oath, relative to the royal session?
Back: 20 June 1789 - three days BEFORE the royal session of 23 June, not a response to it. And it is an Oath, not a 'resolution'. (V2)

Front: TRAP: was eighteenth-century French foreign policy successful?
Back: No. The handout says 'costly but successful' in the same sentence as two lost wars. Read costly and unsuccessful - and note the Austrian Succession was fruitless rather than lost. (V3)

Front: TRAP: how long after 17 June did the clergy join?
Back: Two days - 19 June 1789. The handout prints the unreadable 'This day later'. (V4)

Front: TRAP: date of the Battle of Waterloo?
Back: 18 June 1815. 'June 16-18' describes the campaign; 16 June is Ligny and Quatre Bras. (V5)

Front: TRAP: where was the Parthenopean Republic?
Back: Naples. Piedmont's was the Subalpine Republic. Parthenope is the old Greek name for Naples. (V6)

Front: TRAP: was there a Europe-wide war between 1815 and 1914?
Back: Yes - the Crimean War 1853-56, and the unification wars. The defensible claim is that no GENERAL war involving all the great powers recurred until 1914. (V7)
